steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Primary data is collected firsthand by the investigator for a specific purpose.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Secondary data is data that already exists, collected by someone else for a different purpose.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Methods of collecting primary data include experiments, surveys/questionnaires and observation.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: An experiment involves deliberately changing a variable and measuring the effect (e.g. clinical trials).

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: What is the difference between primary and secondary data? | Q: Name three sources of secondary data. | Q: What is a census?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Primary data is collected firsthand by the investigator for a specific purpose; secondary data already exists and was collected by someone else, usually for a different purpose. | Government databases (e.g. ONS), the internet, books, newspapers, previous studies, company records. | A survey that collects data from every member of the population rather than a sample.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always justify whether primary or secondary data is more appropriate for a given investigation. When evaluating secondary data, comment on its source, date and relevance. A census is different from a sample survey — know when each is appropriate. Observation means watching without interfering — if you change anything, it is an experiment. If an exam question asks about data collection methods, link your choice to the hypothesis.
